stories.title_en: A Trading Companion Turns Thief and Loses His Own Fortune

paragraphs.zh: 张沛，徽州休宁人，大贾也。财本数千两，在瓜州买棉花三百餘担。歙县刘兴，乃孤苦茕民，一向出外肩挑买卖，十餘载未归家，苦积财本七十餘两，亦到此店买棉花。二人同府异县，沛一相见，乡语相同，认为梓里，意气相投，有如兄弟焉。棉花各买毕，同在福建省城陈四店卖，房舍与沛内外。
paragraphs.en: Zhang Pei of Xiuning in Huizhou was a great merchant, with several thousand taels of capital. At Guazhou he bought more than three hundred piculs of cotton. Liu Xing of Shexian was a poor, lonely man. For years he had gone out carrying goods on a shoulder pole; for more than ten years he had not gone home. He had painfully saved a little over seventy taels, and he too came to this shop to buy cotton. The two men were of the same prefecture but different counties. As soon as Pei met him, their local speech matched; he took him for a fellow townsman. Their temperaments agreed, and they were like brothers. When both had finished buying cotton, they sold it together at Chen Si’s shop in the Fujian provincial capital. Their rooms were next to each other, one inner and one outer.

paragraphs.zh: 数日后，兴棉花卖讫。沛者止卖小半，收得银五百餘两。兴见其银，遂起不良念，与本店隔邻孤身一人赵同商议：“我店一客，有银若干。你在南台讨荡船等候，待我拿出来即上船去，随路寻一山庵去躲，与你均分。”赵同许诺。兴佯谓沛曰：“我要同一乡亲到海澄买些南货，今尚未来，要待几日。”一日，有客伙请沛午席，兴将水城挖开，将沛衣箱内银五百餘两，悉偷装在自己行李担内，倩雇一人，说是乡里来催，欲去之速。兴佯曰：“行李收拾已定。奈张兄有人请吃酒，未能辞别。”沛家人曰：“相公一时未归，我代你拜上。”兴即辞主人陈四。陈四亦老练牙人，四顾兴房；兴所挖水城，已将物蔽矣。雇夫佯担海口去，旋即卖踪转南台，来荡船上水口。
paragraphs.en: A few days later Xing sold all his cotton. Pei had sold only a small part, and had taken in more than five hundred taels of silver. When Xing saw that silver, a bad thought rose in him. He talked it over with Zhao Tong, a man living alone next door to the shop: “A guest in my shop has a good deal of silver. You hire a river boat at Nantai and wait. When I bring it out we will board at once, then along the way find a mountain hermitage to hide in, and split it evenly.” Zhao Tong agreed. Xing pretended to tell Pei: “I want to go with a fellow townsman to Haicheng to buy some southern goods. He has not come yet; I will have to wait a few days.” One day a fellow merchant invited Pei to a midday feast. Xing cut a hole through the wall between the rooms, stole all the five hundred-odd taels from Pei’s clothes chest, and packed them into his own carrying loads. He hired a man and said a townsman had come to hurry him, so he needed to leave at once. Xing pretended: “My luggage is already packed. But Brother Zhang has been invited to drink, so I could not say goodbye.” Pei’s servant said: “The master is not back yet; I will give him your respects.” Xing then took leave of the host, Chen Si. Chen Si was a seasoned broker; he looked all around Xing’s room, but the hole Xing had cut was already covered with things. The hired porter pretended to head toward the seaport, then quickly switched tracks, turned to Nantai, and boarded the river boat going up to Shuikou.

paragraphs.zh: 及张沛回，陈四曰：“贵乡里已去矣，托我拜上相公。”沛开房门，看衣箱挖一刀痕，遂曰：“遭瘟！”待开看，银悉偷去。四顾，又无踪迹。陈四入兴房细看，见水城挖开，曰：“了事不得，今无奈了。但相公主仆二人，可雇四名夫，直到海澄。我同一大官，更邀七八人，讨一荡船到水口。”于是陈四往上寻船。至半午后，有船下水来者，问曰：“你一路下来，见一荡船载二人，有行李三箱，上去赶得着否？”艄子曰：“有三人，行李三担，在水口上岸去矣。”荡船赶至将晚方到水口，并未见一人来往。少顷间，见二牧童看牛而归，问曰：“前有三人，行李三担，小官见否？”牧童曰：“其三人入上源垅去矣。”问曰：“那山源有甚乡村？”曰：“无。止有一寺，叫做上源寺。”陈四将银五分，雇一牧童引路，径至其寺，时将三鼓矣。陈四曰：“我等叫他开门，他必逃走。我数人分作两半，一半守前门，一半守后门。天明僧必开门，我等一齐拥入，彼不知逃，方可捉得。”众曰：“说得是。”
paragraphs.en: When Zhang Pei came back, Chen Si said: “Your fellow townsman has already gone. He asked me to give you his respects.” Pei opened the room door, saw a knife-cut on the clothes chest, and said, “Plague take him!” When he opened it, the silver was all gone. He looked all around; there was no trace. Chen Si went into Xing’s room and looked closely, saw the wall cut open, and said: “This cannot be left as it is. There is no other way now. You two, master and servant, can hire four porters and go straight to Haicheng. I will take an officer and invite seven or eight men, hire a river boat, and go to Shuikou.” So Chen Si went upriver looking for a boat. Toward mid-afternoon a boat came downstream. He asked: “All the way down, did you see a river boat carrying two men, with three chests of luggage, going up—can we still catch them?” The boatman said: “There were three men and three loads. They went ashore at Shuikou.” The river boat they hired did not reach Shuikou until nearly evening, and they saw no one coming or going. In a little while they saw two herd-boys bringing cattle home, and asked: “There were three men ahead with three loads—did you young fellows see them?” The boys said: “Those three went into Shangyuan Gully.” They asked: “What villages are in that mountain gully?” The boys said: “None. There is only a temple, called Shangyuan Temple.” Chen Si gave five fen of silver and hired one herd-boy as a guide, and they went straight to the temple. By then it was about the third watch. Chen Si said: “If we call them to open the door, they will surely run. We will split in two: half watch the front door, half the back. At dawn the monks will open; we rush in together, they will not know how to flee, and then we can catch them.” Everyone said: “That is right.”

paragraphs.zh: 及僧开门，众等拥入。和尚惊曰：“众客官哪里来的？”陈四乃道其故，即问：“那三人是甚时候到寺？”僧曰：“到时天色已晚，在那一楼房宿，说他被难，至此逃难。”僧引入，齐拥擒获。见其将沛之银装作一担，自银七十餘两以鼠尾袋装，另藏在身，悉皆搜出。三人跪下求饶：“是我不良，将他银拿来。他者奉还他，我者乞还我。”众等不听他说，将石头乱打半死，行李尽数搬来，三人同系至陈四店内。沛时往海澄，尚未归矣。
paragraphs.en: When the monks opened the door, the whole party rushed in. A monk, startled, said: “Where have you gentlemen come from?” Chen Si told him why they were there, then asked: “What time did those three reach the temple?” The monk said: “They arrived when it was already dark, and are staying in that loft. They said they had met with trouble and had fled here.” The monk led them in; they rushed together and seized them. They saw Pei’s silver packed as one load; Xing’s own seventy-odd taels were in a rat-tail pouch, hidden on his person. All of it was searched out. The three knelt and begged to be spared: “It was our wrongdoing; we took his silver. Give him his back, and please give us ours.” The party would not listen. They beat them half dead with stones, carried all the luggage over, and bound the three back to Chen Si’s shop. Pei had gone toward Haicheng and had not yet returned.

paragraphs.zh: 是日，客伙与地方众等，岂止数千人看，兴之廉耻尽丧。后数日，沛归，谓兴曰：“为你这贼，苦我往返海澄一遭。今幸原银仍在，我也不计较你，今后当做好人。若如汝见，定要呈官究治。”兴曰：“须念乡里二字。”曰：“若说乡里，正被乡里误矣！我念前日久与之情，不计较你，你急前去。”兴曰：“我银乞还我。”但兴银却被众等拿去。沛因叫众等“拿还他，我自谢你。”众人曰：“这贼若告官论，命也难保。今不计较，反敢图赖！”众人又欲殴他，沛劝乃止。谓兴曰：“你心不良，反为若此，今反害己，不足恤也。但我自推心，将银五两与你作盘缠。”兴且感且泣，抱头鼠窜而去。
paragraphs.en: That day fellow merchants and local people—well over a thousand—came to look; Xing’s shame was complete. A few days later Pei returned and said to Xing: “Because of you, you thief, I had a bitter round trip to Haicheng. Luckily the original silver is still here. I will not settle scores with you. From now on be a decent man. If it were as you treated me, I would certainly file a charge and have you punished.” Xing said: “You must think of the two words ‘fellow townsman.’” Pei said: “If we speak of fellow townsmen—I was ruined precisely by a fellow townsman! I remember our old days together, so I will not press it. Get out at once.” Xing said: “Please give me my silver back.” But Xing’s silver had been taken by the crowd. Pei then told them, “Give it back to him; I will thank you myself.” The people said: “If this thief were taken to court, even his life would be hard to keep. You do not even press charges, and he still dares to claim it!” They wanted to beat him again; Pei talked them into stopping. He said to Xing: “Your heart was bad, and it came to this; now you have harmed yourself, and you are not worth pity. But I will open my own heart and give you five taels as travel money.” Xing was grateful and in tears; he covered his head and scurried away.

paragraphs.zh: 噫！久旱甘雨，他乡故知。客于外者，一见乡里，朝夕与游，即成绸缪之交，有如兄弟者，人之情也。沛之与兴，以同郡乡人，又同兹贸易，与之共店托处，亦处旅者之势然也。何兴之包藏祸心，同室操戈，利其财而盗之？彼之暗渡荡船，自谓得计；岂知天理昭彰。奸盗不容，卒之擒获丛殴，噬脐无及，数十年苦积七十金，一旦失之。图未得之财，丧已获之利，何其愚也！予深有慨焉，故笔之，以为奸贪丧心者戒，而因告商者之宜慎，勿如乡里之为盗者误也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Alas! Rain after a long drought; an old acquaintance in a strange land. A man sojourning abroad, once he meets a fellow townsman, goes about with him morning and evening and soon forms a close bond, like brothers—that is human feeling. Pei and Xing were men of the same prefecture, in the same trade, sharing an inn and lodging together; that too is how travelers are placed. How could Xing hide a vicious heart, turn the blade on a roommate, and steal for the sake of the money? He slipped onto a river boat in secret and thought himself clever; he did not know Heaven’s principle is bright. Treachery and theft are not tolerated. In the end he was caught and beaten by the crowd, too late for regret. Seventy taels painfully saved over several decades were lost in a single morning. He schemed for wealth he did not yet have, and lost the profit he already held—how foolish! I am deeply moved, so I write this down as a warning to the treacherous and greedy who have lost their conscience, and to tell merchants they should be careful, and not be misled by a “fellow townsman” who is in fact a thief.

stories.title_en: Pride Starts a Lawsuit and Costs Him Fortune and Life

paragraphs.zh: 魏邦材，广东客人，富冠一省。为人骄傲非常，辄夸巨富。出外为商，无人可入其目。一日，在湖州买丝一百担，转往本省去卖，在杭州讨大船，共客商二十餘人同船。因风有阻，在富阳县五七日。其仆屡天早争先炊饭，船中往来，略不如意，辄与众斗口。众皆以伙计相聚日知，况材亢傲而相让之，其仆亦倚主势，日与众忤。在邦材，当抑仆而慰同侪可也；反党其仆，屡出言不逊曰：“你这一起下等下流，哪一个来与我和？”动以千金为言。又曰：“一船之货，我一人可买。”如此言者数次，众皆不堪，大恨之。
paragraphs.en: Wei Bangcai was a Guangdong merchant, the richest in the province. He was extraordinarily arrogant and always boasted of his great wealth. When he went out to trade, no one was worth a glance in his eyes. One day he bought a hundred piculs of silk in Huzhou, to take back to his own province to sell. In Hangzhou he hired a large boat; more than twenty merchants shared it. The wind held them up, and they stayed in Fuyang County five to seven days. His servants always rushed to cook first at dawn; as they came and went on the boat, if anything was slightly not to their liking they wrangled with the others. Everyone else, as partners thrown together for days, and besides because Bangcai was so high and mighty, yielded to them; the servants also leaned on their master’s power and clashed with people daily. Bangcai ought to have checked his servants and soothed his companions; instead he took his servants’ side, and more than once spoke insolently: “You pack of low, inferior types—which of you will come and compete with me?” He always talked in thousands of taels. He also said: “I could buy this whole boat’s cargo by myself.” He said such things several times. Everyone found it unbearable and hated him deeply.

paragraphs.zh: 时有徽州汪逢七，乃巨族显宦世家也。不忿材以财势压人，曰：“世长势短，辄以千金为言。昔石崇之富，岂出公之下哉？而后竟何如也？”材怒其敌己，曰：“船中有长于下流者，有本大于下流者，竟无一言，你敢挺出与我作对？以丝一百担，价值数千金，统与你和。”逢七骂曰：“这下流好不知趣！屡屡无状，真不知死小辈也。我有数千金与你和，叫你无命归故士！”二人争口不休。众皆暗喜汪魏角胜，中心大快。有爱汪者，相劝各自入仓。
paragraphs.en: At the time there was Wang Fengqi of Huizhou, from a great clan of prominent officials. He would not stand Bangcai using money and power to crush people, and said: “Fortune in this world rises and falls, yet you always talk in thousands of taels. In former days, was Shi Chong’s wealth any less than yours? And what became of him later?” Bangcai was angry that someone would match him, and said: “On this boat there are men senior to you lowlifes, and men with more capital than you lowlifes, and they have not said a word. You dare step out and stand against me? I will stake the whole hundred piculs of silk, worth several thousand taels, against you.” Fengqi cursed him: “You low creature, you truly do not know your place! Again and again you behave outrageously—you really are a little wretch who does not know he can die. I have several thousand taels to match you, and I will see you have no life left to return to your native soil!” The two wrangled without stopping. Everyone secretly delighted that Wang and Wei were locking horns, and were greatly pleased at heart. Someone who sided with Wang urged them each to go into their own cabins.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，李汉卿背云：“幸得汪兄为对。”材听之，乃骂汉卿而及逢七，语甚不逊，大都材出言极伤众。众不甘而忿恨曰：“一船人却被一人欺！我等歃血为盟，与他定夺！”逢七曰：“众等帮我，等我与他作对，以泄众等恨也。他有丝一百担，众助我打他半死，他必去告状，我搬他丝另藏一处。留一半，方好与他对官，将其底帐灭之。他若告我，众不可星散，坚言证之，即将他丝卖来与他使。俗云‘穿他衫，拜他年’。斗殴之讼，岂比人命重情？”众曰：“说得是。我等皆欲报忿，戒勿漏泄。”布谋已定。逢七乃与材在船中相殴数次，材极受亏，奔告在县，状已准矣。
paragraphs.en: The next day Li Hanqing said behind Wei’s back: “Luckily we have Brother Wang to stand up to him.” Bangcai heard it, and cursed Hanqing and then Fengqi, in most insolent language; in the main, Bangcai’s words cut the whole company deeply. They would not swallow it, and said in anger: “A whole boat of people bullied by one man! We will smear blood and swear an alliance, and settle it with him!” Fengqi said: “You all help me. Let me stand against him, and vent everyone’s hatred. He has a hundred piculs of silk. Help me beat him half dead; he will certainly go and file a charge. We will move his silk and hide it somewhere else. Leave half, so we can face him in court, and destroy his account books. If he sues me, you must not scatter; hold firm and testify. Then we will sell his silk and use it against him. As the saying goes, ‘Wear his shirt to keep his New Year.’ A brawl in court is hardly a homicide case.” Everyone said: “That is right. We all want to pay back the insult. Swear not to leak it.” The plot was set. Fengqi then fought Bangcai several times on the boat; Bangcai got the worst of it, ran to the county to sue, and the plaint was accepted.

paragraphs.zh: 逢七将材丝挑去一半藏讫，以材买丝底帐、各处税票悉皆灭矣。自己货发落在牙人张春店内。材上船见丝搬去，乃大与逢七殴；即补状，复告抢丝五十担，以一船客伙、艄公作证。逢七以猪血涂头，令二人抬入衙内，告急救人命事抵。即将银一百两，投本县抽丰官客，系本县霍爷母舅。材将银一百五十两，投本县进士魏贤及春元九位。逢七又将银二百两，亦投此数人。进士魏贤等先见本县为魏，又后催书，言辞支离，两下都不合矣。及审一起干证，艄公齐说：“相殴是实，未见搬丝。”本县判断担丝情捏，只以争殴致讼，俱各不合。材不甘，又赴本道告，批与本府推官陈爷审问。二人俱有分上，依县原审回招。材又奔大巡军门各司道告，及南京刑部告。然文状不离原词，皆因（袭）原断。
paragraphs.en: Fengqi had half of Bangcai’s silk carried off and hidden, and destroyed Bangcai’s silk-purchase ledgers and the tax receipts from every station. His own goods he lodged at broker Zhang Chun’s shop. When Bangcai went on board and saw the silk gone, he fought Fengqi hard; he filed a supplementary plaint, further charging robbery of fifty piculs of silk, and named a boatful of fellow merchants and the boatman as witnesses. Fengqi smeared pig blood on his head, had two men carry him into the yamen, and filed a countercharge of a life-and-death emergency. He then sent a hundred taels to a hanger-on in the county who milks official connections, who was Magistrate Huo’s maternal uncle. Bangcai sent a hundred and fifty taels to Metropolitan Graduate Wei Xian of the county and to nine provincial graduates. Fengqi then also sent two hundred taels to the same men. Wei Xian and the others first went to the magistrate on Wei’s behalf; later urging letters came, their language became inconsistent, and they no longer fitted either side. When the whole set of witnesses was examined, the boatman and they all said: “The fighting was real; we did not see silk being moved.” The county judged the claim about piculs of silk to be fabricated; it was only a quarrel that led to a suit; both sides were in the wrong. Bangcai would not accept it, and appealed to the circuit; the case was assigned to Prefectural Judge Chen. Both men had connections; the report followed the county’s original finding. Bangcai then ran to the grand inspector, the military governor, every circuit office, and even the Nanjing Ministry of Justice. But the papers never left the original wording, so all followed the original judgment.

paragraphs.zh: 二人争讼一年许，材前餘丝皆已用尽。材叫一亲兄来帮讼，带银五百餘两，亦多用去。材又患病店中，家中叫一亲叔来看。其人乃忠厚长者，询其来历，始知侄为人亢傲，乃致此也。众客商说出此事，要作和气处息，各出银一百两，收拾官府，内抽五十两，与材作盘费之资而归。材归，自思为商之日，带出许多财物，今空手回家，不胜愤郁；且受合家讪詈，益增呕气。未几发疽，数月而死。
paragraphs.en: The two men sued each other for about a year. Bangcai’s remaining silk was all spent. He called an elder brother to come help with the suit; the brother brought more than five hundred taels, which were also mostly used up. Bangcai then fell ill at the inn. The family called a paternal uncle to come see him. The man was an honest, thick elder. He asked how it had started, and only then learned that the nephew’s arrogant ways had brought this on. The merchants told the whole affair and wanted a peaceful settlement: each side would put up a hundred taels to settle with the officials, and fifty taels would be taken from that for Bangcai as travel money home. Bangcai went home, thought of how much goods and money he had taken out in his trading days, and now was returning empty-handed; he could not bear the anger and gloom. He was also mocked and scolded by the whole household, which only added to his sick rage. Before long a carbuncle broke out; in a few months he died.

paragraphs.zh: 噫！邦材以巨富自恃，想其待童仆与乡人也。酷虐暴戾，人皆让之，酿成桀骜之性，是亢极而不知返者也。一旦出外为商，井蛙痴子，眼孔不宏，呶呶贯钱，知有己而不知有人，口角无惩，致逢七等忿而布谋，搬丝诘讼。始自挟其财多，可投分上凌人，意谓逢七等皆在其掌股玩弄矣；殊知县、府、道、司、刑部遍告，财本俱空，皆不能胜。斯时也，羝羊角藩，抑郁成疾，悔无及矣。非伊叔见机收拾归家，几郁死于外，作他乡之鬼矣。“谦受益，满招损”，自古记之。故匹夫胜予，无以国骄人。圣人之训，三致意焉。即王公大人，矜骄贾灭，比比皆然，况夫公么之辈乎！即庭闱密迩，傲惰而辟，已为非宜，况处羁旅之地乎！为商者，寄寡亲之境，群异乡之人，刚柔得中，止而丽明，尚恐意外之变，而可以傲临人乎！故曰：和以处众，四海之内皆兄弟；满以自骄，舟中之人皆敌国。商者鉴此，可以自省矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Alas! Bangcai relied on being hugely rich. Think how he treated servants and fellow villagers: cruel, violent, overbearing. Everyone yielded to him, and that bred a savage stubbornness; he had reached the extreme of arrogance and did not know how to turn back. Once he went out to trade, he was a frog-in-a-well fool, with a narrow eye; he rattled on about money, knew himself and not others, and never checked his tongue. That drove Fengqi and the rest to fury and to lay a plot, move the silk, and drag him into court. At first he leaned on having much money, thinking he could buy influence and crush people, and supposed Fengqi and the others were in the palm of his hand. He did not know that after appeals through county, prefecture, circuit, the offices, and the Ministry of Justice, his capital would all be gone and he still could not win. By then he was a ram with its horns stuck in the fence; gloom made him ill, and regret came too late. If his uncle had not seen the moment to wrap it up and send him home, he would nearly have died of misery abroad and become a ghost in a strange land. “Humility brings benefit; fullness invites loss”—this has been recorded since ancient times. So even if a commoner outdoes you, do not swagger over others on the strength of rank or state. The Sage’s teaching returns to this again and again. Even princes and great men, time after time, have pride purchase their ruin—how much more so ordinary private men! Even in the inner rooms among close kin, arrogance and slackness that go off the path are already wrong—how much more in a place of sojourn! A merchant lodges in a region with few kin, among people from other parts. Keep hardness and softness in balance, stay still and cling to clarity, and you still fear an unexpected turn—can you then look down on people with pride? So it is said: treat the many with harmony, and all within the four seas are brothers; swell with pride, and even the people in your boat become an enemy state. Merchants should look at this and examine themselves.

stories.title_en: Chair Carriers Lead a Boy Candidate into the Hills

paragraphs.zh: 超世材，建阳人也。年方垂髫，往府应茂才之选，未取而归。以行李三担，雇挑费大，乃寄船中，命仆护之。己独于陆路轿行，只一日可归。在路雇轿时，打开银包，取二钱碎银与之。两轿夫从旁看窥，有银一大锭。不行上三十里，扛入山僻路去。超生曰：“我昨从船往府，此陆路虽今日初行，但官路须是往来通途，不当在此偏僻去处。”轿夫曰：“正是此去，望前便大官道矣。”又行，更入山径。超生心悟，即呼曰：“我知此不是大路。你们不过是要银，我身上只一锭银三两。我家富万金，只我一人，便把此三银子送你不妨，何必要起歹意？”二轿夫放下，曰：“如此便把来与我，免你一命。”超生笑解付之，曰：“此何大事，而作此举动？好小器！可送我还大路。”二轿夫不顾，得了银，径从山路奔去。
paragraphs.en: Chao Shicai was a man of Jianyang. He was still a child with his hair in tufts. He went to the prefecture for the licentiate selection, was not chosen, and headed home. He had three loads of luggage; hiring porters would cost a great deal, so he left them on a boat and ordered a servant to watch them. He himself went by land in a sedan chair; it was only one day’s trip home. When he hired the chair on the road, he opened his silver packet and took out two qian of broken silver to pay them. The two chair men peeked from the side: there was one large ingot. Before they had gone thirty li, they carried him onto a lonely mountain path. Young Chao said: “Yesterday I went to the prefecture by boat. Though I am on this land road for the first time today, an official road should be a through-route with traffic; we should not be in this out-of-the-way place.” The chair men said: “This is the way; look ahead and you will hit the main official road.” They went on, still further into mountain tracks. Young Chao understood, and called out: “I know this is not the main road. You only want the silver. I have on me only one ingot of three taels. My family is worth ten thousand taels, and I am an only son, so giving you these three taels is no matter—why turn to harm?” The two chair men set him down and said: “Then hand it over, and we will spare your life.” Young Chao smiled, undid it and gave it to them, saying: “What a fuss over so little—how petty! Now take me back to the main road.” The two chair men paid no heed; once they had the silver they ran off through the hills.

paragraphs.zh: 超生自还寻大路，行至路边店舍，问此处有某县人开店否？人指示之，即入，对店主曰：“我系超某家，因雇轿夫，被其谋去盘缠银，又不能徒步走路。汝若识我家，托代雇两轿夫，送我到家，加还其工钱。”店主曰：“尊府大家，人皆闻名，我岂不知？”即奉上午饭，命两轿夫送回。归家言被谋之事，及某店归之情，家中大喜，曰：“得不遭毒手，幸矣！三两银何足惜！”因厚款二轿夫，仍专人往谢其店。
paragraphs.en: Young Chao found his own way back to the main road. He came to a roadside inn and asked whether anyone from such-and-such county kept a shop here. People pointed it out. He went in and said to the innkeeper: “I am of the Chao family. I hired chair men and they plotted and took my travel silver, and I cannot walk the rest of the way. If you know my family, please hire two chair men to send me home; we will pay extra wages.” The innkeeper said: “Yours is a great house; everyone has heard the name. How would I not know?” He served him a midday meal at once and ordered two chair men to take him back. When he reached home he told of the plot and of how that shop had sent him. The family was overjoyed and said: “Lucky you did not fall into their murderous hands! What are three taels worth grieving over?” So they treated the two chair men generously, and still sent someone specially to thank that inn.

paragraphs.zh: 按：超生初未晓此路程，但见扛入山僻，即知非是大路。察两人谋害之情，便捐银与之，免遭毒手。不然，命且不保，安能存银？又知寻本乡店主，托雇轿送归，方保泰然无危。此其年虽幼稚，而才智过人远矣。诗曰：“书显官人才，书添君子智。”令超生非读书明理，几何不蹈于陷井？
paragraphs.en: Note: Young Chao did not know this route at first, but as soon as they carried him into the hills he knew it was not the main road. He saw that the two meant harm, so he gave up the silver and escaped with his life. Otherwise he might not have kept his life—how could the silver remain? He also knew to find an innkeeper from his own county and have chairs hired to send him home, and so came through in safety. Young in years, his resourcefulness far outstripped others. As the verse says: “Books make talented men into officials; books add wisdom to a gentleman.” Had young Chao not read and understood principle, how far would he have been from stepping into the pit?

stories.title_en: He Insists on a High Price and Misses the Market

paragraphs.zh: 于定志，云南西河县人。为人心贪性执，冒昧于利。一日，买栀子往四川处卖，得银八十餘两。复买当归、川芎，往江西樟树卖，每担止着本脚银二两六钱。到时，归、芎虽缺，然比前价稍落些。牙人代发当归，十两一担；川芎六两一担。定志怒责牙人曰：“前日十二两价，如何减许多？”牙人辩曰：“若到二三担，则可依前价；今到二十餘担，若从前价，何以服行情？公欲重价，凭公发别店卖之，何必怒焉？”定志与牙角口，旁有一客伙张淳者，劝曰：“公货获利三倍，当要见机。倘价若落，未免有失渡无船之悔矣。”定志坚执不听。
paragraphs.en: Yu Dingzhi was a man of Xihe County in Yunnan. He was greedy at heart and stubborn by nature, reckless after profit. One day he bought gardenia, took it to Sichuan to sell, and got more than eighty taels. He then bought danggui and chuanxiong, to sell at Zhangshu in Jiangxi; each picul had only two taels six qian of cost including freight. When he arrived, danggui and chuanxiong were still scarce, but the price had fallen a little from before. The broker sold danggui for him at ten taels a picul, and chuanxiong at six taels a picul. Dingzhi angrily blamed the broker: “The other day the price was twelve taels—why cut so much?” The broker answered: “If two or three piculs had arrived, we could follow the old price. Now more than twenty piculs have come; if we used the old price, how would that match the market? If you want a high price, take it to another shop yourself and sell—why get angry?” Dingzhi wrangled with the broker. A fellow merchant standing by, Zhang Chun, advised: “Your goods already triple the money; you should watch the moment. If the price falls, you will regret missing the ferry when no boat is left.” Dingzhi held firm and would not listen.

paragraphs.zh: 数日后，到有当归三四担，牙人发价十两卖讫。淳又劝之曰：“此客已卖十两价耳，公何不卖也？”彼亦不听。后又二客人，有十五担到，牙人发价七两，亦卖讫。过数日，又有十餘担来，止卖四两。定志暗悔无及，众客又背地代他扼腕。定志又坐一月餘，价落货贱，与牙人不合，遂转发到福建建宁府，止卖三两七钱一担，比樟树价又减，更废船脚又多。定志自恨命薄，不当赚钱。人谓其非命薄也，乃心高也；非挫时也，乃过贪也。故笔之，以为嗜利不饱者鉴。
paragraphs.en: A few days later three or four piculs of danggui arrived; the broker sold them at ten taels and they were gone. Chun advised him again: “That merchant already sold at ten taels—why do you not sell?” He still would not listen. Later two more merchants arrived with fifteen piculs; the broker sold them at seven taels, and they too were gone. After a few more days, another ten-odd piculs came, and sold at only four taels. Dingzhi secretly regretted too late; the other merchants also wrung their wrists for him behind his back. Dingzhi sat another month and more; prices fell and the goods were cheap. He fell out with the broker, so he forwarded the lot to Jianning Prefecture in Fujian, and sold at only three taels seven qian a picul—lower still than the Zhangshu price, and more boat freight wasted besides. Dingzhi cursed his thin luck, that he was not meant to make money. People said it was not thin luck but a high heart; not bad timing but too much greed. So I write this down as a mirror for those whose thirst for profit is never filled.

paragraphs.zh: 按：商为利而奔驰南北，谁不欲广收多获？特遇时而倍得其利，便可见机发脱。何乃贪黩无厌，至失机会而后扼腕，何益哉？甚矣，贪之为害也！不知凡物贱极征贵，贵极征贱，必无极而不返之理。此阴阳消长之数、造化否泰之机，往往皆然。岂可违时而遂贪心乎？是以从古君子，以不贪为宝。
paragraphs.en: Note: Merchants race north and south for profit; who does not want a wide take and a big haul? But when the times let you double what you put in, you should see the moment and sell. Why be endlessly greedy, and only wring your wrists after the chance is gone—what good is that? How harmful greed is! They do not know that when a thing is extremely cheap it trends toward dear, and when extremely dear it trends toward cheap; there is no extreme that does not turn back. This is the waxing and waning of yin and yang, the rise and fall in creation’s mechanism—so it always is. How can you go against the time to feed a greedy heart? That is why gentlemen from of old have taken not-greed as their treasure.

stories.title_en: Posing as an Exam Candidate, They Lease a House and Loot a Widow

paragraphs.zh: 会城中，每逢科试之年，各府举子到者极多。不论大小房屋，举子俱出重租，暂僦以居。东街王寡妇，其先得丹穴擅利，数世积镪巨万，名闻于人。止生二子，一弱冠，一垂髫。内止一丫头，外用一仆代管家，一小厮供役使，不过五六人家口。其厅堂高敞，房舍深广。其外厢每科租与举子居，常收厚利。
paragraphs.en: In the provincial capital, every year of the provincial examinations, candidates from the prefectures arrived in great numbers. Houses large and small were all let at a heavy rent, taken for a short stay. Widow Wang of East Street—her ancestors had grown rich from a cinnabar mine, and several generations had piled up cash by the tens of thousands; the name was known. She had only two sons, one just capped, one still a child. Inside there was only one maid; outside she used one servant as steward and a page for errands—no more than five or six mouths in the house. The halls were high and open, the rooms deep and wide. The outer wings she rented each examination year to candidates, and often took in a thick profit.

paragraphs.zh: 辛卯七月初，举子纷至。忽有二家仆，冠服齐楚，来择屋居。王管家引其看左右厅房，皆清幽洁净。二家仆曰：“此屋光明宽大，可中公子意。我全租之，不可再租他人。敢问租金多少？”王管家曰：“往年众人共租，租金常二十两。今你一家租，人少，不乱杂，只十五两亦可。”二家仆还十二两，即以现银付讫。一仆出引公子，乘四轿，带四仆并一小厮来。行李五六担，皆精好物件。到即以土仪送家主，又值银二三两。王寡妇曰：“往年举子送人事皆淡薄，今这公子真方家手面。”次日，命管家排大筵席，敬请公子，二子出陪。公子放怀欢饮，二更方散。
paragraphs.en: In the first part of the seventh month of a xinmao year, candidates poured in. Suddenly two family servants, hat and clothes neat and fine, came to choose rooms. Steward Wang showed them the halls and rooms to left and right; all were quiet, secluded, and clean. The two servants said: “These rooms are bright and spacious; they will suit our young master. We will rent the whole of them; you must not rent to anyone else. May we ask how much the rent is?” Steward Wang said: “In past years when many men shared the rent, it was often twenty taels. Now your one household is renting, fewer people, not a mixed crowd—fifteen taels will do.” The two servants offered twelve taels, and paid the cash on the spot. One servant went out and brought the young master, who came in a four-bearer sedan with four servants and a page. There were five or six loads of luggage, all fine things. On arrival he sent local gifts to the householder, worth another two or three taels. Widow Wang said: “In past years candidates’ gifts were all thin; this young master truly has a great house’s style.” The next day she ordered the steward to lay a large feast, respectfully invited the young master, and had her two sons come out to keep him company. The young master drank freely and happily; they did not break up until the second watch.

paragraphs.zh: 又次日，公子遣家仆叫厨子来做酒回席。一席请二幼主，一席送入内堂，与主母饮，叫其丫头边陪。命一小厮入，洒酒侍奉。一小席待两管家者，四仆陪之。各饮至二更，公子曰：“带来的酒开来饮。”少顷暖至，其酒味香甜，又不甚严，极是好饮。公子斟两大杯，奉二子曰：“此酒略爽口，各奉三杯。”二子各领饮。小厮在内，亦斟与主母饮。四仆亦劝两管家饮。二更已尽，赍发厨子去，收拾闭门讫。其后所奉酒内放陀陀花，其药性到，将一家人皆昏倒。假公子并六家仆，将寡妇等绑住，夤夜搜其财物，尽数收拾作五六担。晨钟一鸣，开大门公然挑去，并无人知。
paragraphs.en: The day after that, the young master sent a servant to call a cook to make a return feast. One table invited the two young masters of the house; one table was sent into the inner hall for the mistress to drink, with her maid sitting by. He ordered a page to go in and pour wine and wait on them. A small table treated the two stewards, with the four servants sitting with them. Each party drank until the second watch. The young master said: “Open the wine we brought and drink that.” In a little while it was warmed and brought; it tasted fragrant and sweet, and was not too harsh—excellent to drink. The young master poured two large cups and presented them to the two sons: “This wine is a little easier on the mouth; take three cups each.” The two sons each drank. Inside, the page also poured for the mistress. The four servants also pressed the two stewards to drink. When the second watch was over, they paid off the cook, tidied up, and shut the doors. In the wine served later they had put datura blossoms. When the drug took hold, the whole household collapsed in a stupor. The fake young master and six servants bound the widow and the rest, searched their goods through the night, and packed everything into five or six loads. At the first stroke of the morning bell they opened the great gate and carried it all out in full view; no one knew.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，至午左右，邻居见其门大开，无一人来往，相邀入看，一家人皆被捆倒，如醉未醒。曰：“此必中毒被劫。”急代请医，解去其毒方醒，乃言被假公子租屋，投毒夜动。及寻究之，茫无跳影矣。
paragraphs.en: The next day, around noon, the neighbors saw the gate wide open and not a person coming or going. They invited one another in to look: the whole household was bound and down, as if drunk and not yet awake. They said: “They must have been poisoned and robbed.” They hurriedly called a doctor for them; only after the poison was drawn off did they wake, and then they told how a fake young master had rented the rooms, given them a drug, and struck at night. When people tried to track the robbers, there was not a shadow left.

paragraphs.zh: 按：科举租屋，历科皆然，谁知有大棍行此术？其欲独租，不令租他人，犹是常情；惟初至时送厚人事，主必设席相待，理固然也；旋即回席，又且甚丰，一家婢仆皆有酒，即有意投毒矣。善察者，于送人事时犹是难察；惟一家大小皆有酒席相待，此处宜参透之。彼以客回主席，何必并及内外贵贱人哉？然孀妇女流之辈，二子黄口娃儿；若两管家者，彼能以是而预防之，则棍何得而行劫乎！
paragraphs.en: Note: Renting rooms for the examinations has been so in every session; who knew a big crook would work this trick? Wanting to rent the whole place, and not let it to others, is still ordinary feeling. Sending generous gifts on first arrival, so that the host must lay a feast, is also in the nature of things. Then at once a return feast, and a lavish one, with wine for every maid and servant in the house—that was already the intent to drug them. A good observer would still find the gifts hard to see through; but when every person in the household, high and low, is given a feast, that is the place to see through it. He is a guest returning the host’s courtesy—why should that reach everyone inside and out, noble and menial? Still, a widow is only a woman, and the two sons yellow-mouthed children; as for the two stewards, had they guarded against this, how could the crooks have carried out the robbery?

stories.title_en: A Sham Cargo Is Used to Raid a Pawnshop

paragraphs.zh: 县衙边有一大典当铺，贮积货物巨万。人以物件当者，不拘多少，皆能收之。一日，有客人容貌雄伟，径入堂内相拜，屏人语曰：“不敢相瞒，吾是异府人，常做君子生意，屡年积得器物甚多。前月拦得赃官七个柜，多有宝贝器玩。今幸藏到贵县，一时难以变卖。尊府若能收当，愿面估其值，以十分之一先交与我，待你卖后均分其价，每千两各得五百，明年对月来支。”店主曰：“愿借货物一看。”贼曰：“货物极多，共九大柜，外面难以开看。今夜须吩咐守城者勿闭门，待人定后，你雇十八人在船边来抬入宝店，当面看定，估计价值，两相交付。先求些现，餘者明年找完。”店主曰：“可。”夜间吩咐守城者留门，雇十八人往江边扛货。果抬九柜入店。
paragraphs.en: Beside the county yamen there was a large pawnshop, with goods stored by the tens of thousands. When people brought things to pawn, no matter how much, it could take them all in. One day a guest of imposing looks went straight into the hall, made a bow, sent others away, and said: “I will not hide it from you. I am from another prefecture. I make my living as a highwayman, and over the years I have piled up a great many objects. Last month I intercepted seven chests belonging to a corrupt official; there are many treasures and curios. Now luckily I have hidden them in your county, but I cannot sell them all at once. If your house can take them in pawn, I am willing to estimate the value face to face; give me one tenth first. After you sell, we split the price evenly—five hundred of every thousand taels each—and next year in the same month I will come to collect.” The shopkeeper said: “I would like to borrow a look at the goods.” The thief said: “There are a great many goods, nine large chests in all; they cannot be opened outside. Tonight you must tell the city-gate guards not to shut the gate. After people have settled, hire eighteen men to come to the boat and carry them into your precious shop. We will look them over on the spot, estimate the value, and exchange. I ask some cash first; the rest we will settle next year.” The shopkeeper said: “Agreed.” At night he told the gate guards to leave the gate open, and hired eighteen men to go to the river to carry the goods. Sure enough they carried nine chests into the shop.

paragraphs.zh: 赍发扛夫去讫，闭上外门。贼将锁匙将九柜锁都开讫，喝一声曰：“速出来！”每柜二人，各执短刀突出，将店主绑住，曰：“略做声便杀！”十九人争入内，把其男女都绑缚，然后将其铺内货物，尽数收入九柜内。十九人分抬出城，再嘱守城者曰：“可锁门矣。”夤夜扛上船去。半夜后，有渐解开绑者，因出解家人之缚，赶至城门，门已闭矣。问曰：“汝见扛柜者否？”守城人应曰：“扛柜者出城多时矣。”五鼓门开，寻至江边，贼夤夜开船，杳不知去向矣。
paragraphs.en: They paid off the porters and shut the outer door. The thief took a key and opened all nine chest locks, then shouted: “Come out at once!” Two men from each chest, each with a short blade, burst out, bound the shopkeeper, and said: “Make a sound and we kill you!” Nineteen men rushed inside, bound all the men and women, then packed the shop’s goods into the nine chests. The nineteen split the loads and carried them out of the city, then told the gate guards: “You may lock the gate now.” Through the night they carried them onto a boat. After midnight someone gradually worked his bonds loose, then went and freed the rest of the household. They ran to the city gate; the gate was already shut. They asked: “Did you see the men carrying chests?” The gate guard answered: “The chest-carriers left the city a good while ago.” At the fifth watch the gate opened. They searched to the river; the thieves had cast off in the night, and no one knew where they had gone.

paragraphs.zh: 按：一人来店，其柜皆系自雇人抬入，谁知防之？但彼既称九柜，何不日间躬到其船，面察其柜内货物，则贼计无所施矣。顾听其夜来，又嘱守城者留门以延之入，致堕贼计，是开门而揖盗也。谅哉，利令智昏矣！
paragraphs.en: Note: One man came to the shop; the chests were carried in by men he himself hired—who would guard against that? But since he claimed nine chests, why not go to the boat yourself in daylight and look at the goods inside? Then the thieves would have had no play. Instead he let them come at night, and even told the gate guards to leave the gate open to let them in, and so fell into the plot: that is opening the door and bowing the robbers in. Truly, profit makes wisdom drunk!

stories.title_en: A Horseman Grabs Silver in a Nanjing Shop

paragraphs.zh: 董荣，山东人也。往南京廊下邓铺中买丝绸三匹，价银四两四钱。以天平对定，只差银色，讲议未成。忽一人骑白马，戴笼巾，穿青绢双摆，亦来铺买绸。邓店以绸与看。其人将董荣的绸来看：曰：“吾为你二家折衷。”叫董荣再添银二钱，荣意亦肯添。其人接银过手看，一跳上马，加鞭而行，马走如飞。荣忙赶上，过一巷，转一弯，其人与马俱不见踪。无奈，再至邓铺，谓其与棍相套，互争扭打。
paragraphs.en: Dong Rong was a man of Shandong. He went to Deng’s shop in the Langxia corridors of Nanjing to buy three bolts of silk, at a price of four taels four qian. The balance scale was already agreed; they only differed on the quality of the silver, and the deal was not yet made. Suddenly a man riding a white horse, wearing a cage-hat and a blue silk double-flap robe, also came to the shop to buy silk. Deng’s shop showed him silk. The man took Dong Rong’s silk to look at and said: “I will split the difference for you two.” He told Dong Rong to add two qian more; Rong was willing to add it. The man took the silver in hand to look, then sprang onto the horse, laid on the whip, and the horse flew. Rong hurried after him, went down an alley, turned a corner—man and horse were both gone. He had no choice but to go back to Deng’s shop, saying the shop was in cahoots with the crook; they wrangled and came to blows.

paragraphs.zh: 忽巡街刘御史到，二人皆拦街口告。御史带回衙，拘其左邻右舍来审。邻舍曰：“先是荣入铺买绸，只争银色未成。一棍忽骑马至，亦称买绸，自言为彼二家折衷，叫荣添银。棍把其银入手，一跳上马而去，荣忙赶未见。以故二人争打，告在天台。谅此棍正是响马贼，必非通同店家作弊者。”刘爷曰：“邻佑所证是实，此非店家通同者。但在伊店而遭失脱，合令邓店补还银二两二钱，董荣亦自认二两二钱。”发出依处，彼此无罪。
paragraphs.en: Suddenly Censor Liu, on street patrol, arrived; both men blocked his way in the street to complain. The censor took them back to his yamen and summoned the left and right neighbors to hear the case. The neighbors said: “First Rong came into the shop to buy silk; they only differed on the silver’s quality and had not closed. A crook suddenly rode up, also claiming to buy silk, said he would split the difference for the two of them, and told Rong to add silver. The crook got the silver in his hand, sprang onto the horse and left; Rong hurried after and saw nothing. That is why the two fought and complained before Your Honor. This crook was surely a mounted highwayman; he cannot have been in league with the shop.” His Honor Liu said: “The neighbors’ testimony is true; this was not a shop collusion. But the loss happened in his shop, so Deng’s shop should make good two taels two qian, and Dong Rong should also bear two taels two qian himself.” They were sent out under this settlement; neither was found guilty.

paragraphs.zh: 按：响马贼尝在林路僻处动夺行旅，飞马而去。今在京城中行此，亦大奇也。且彼衣冠既美，有马在旁，其谁防之？今后上店买物，或有异色人在旁，须当严防，勿使银入人手，是亦老实照管之一策也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Mounted highwaymen usually strike travelers on lonely forest roads and gallop off. To do this inside the capital is also a rare wonder. And he was well dressed, with a horse beside him—who would guard against him? From now on, when you go into a shop to buy, if a strange-looking person is standing by, you must watch strictly, and not let silver pass into another man’s hand. That too is one honest way of looking after yourself.

stories.title_en: A Secret Seal-Stamp Wins a Travel Roll in Court

paragraphs.zh: 乡有尤刁民者，侮法健讼，渔猎下民。人闻其刁风，莫不畏而远之。一日，往府搭船，已先入船坐。后搭船者群至，萍水相逢，彼此各不相识，船中对坐漫谈。忽讲及按院拿刁民事。内有姓丘后生，不知尤刁民之在船也，与众曰：“闻此时本县唯尤五最刁，凡与人暂处，无不被其骗害者。若得按院除了此人，民亦安生。”尤五心中冷笑，谓“吾与尔何干，既扬我刁，又愿按院除我？此人若不白骗他一场，枉得此刁名也。”见丘生所带铺陈甚好，即取一木印，挨近其毡条白处，私打一印号于中。
paragraphs.en: In the countryside there was a man called You the Shyster, who mocked the law, loved lawsuits, and preyed on lesser people. When people heard of his litigious ways, none but feared him and kept away. One day he took a boat to the prefecture, and was already seated on board. Later passengers came in a crowd; they were chance meetings on the water, none knew one another, and they sat facing each other chatting. Suddenly the talk turned to the touring censor rounding up litigious bullies. Among them was a young man surnamed Qiu, who did not know that You the Shyster was on the boat. He said to the others: “I hear that in our county right now You Wu is the most litigious of all. Anyone who is with him even a short while is cheated and harmed. If the touring censor would get rid of this man, the people could live in peace.” You Wu laughed coldly to himself: “What have I to do with you, that you spread my shyster name and even wish the censor to get rid of me? If I do not cheat this man openly, I will have this shyster name for nothing.” He saw that Young Qiu had very fine bedding, so he took a wood seal, drew near a white place on the felt, and secretly stamped a mark in the middle.

paragraphs.zh: 船晚至岸，各收拾自己行李而去。尤刁民尾丘生之后，行至府前，在仆担头把铺陈抢下，曰：“多劳你挑，我自拖去。”丘生来抢，曰：“是我铺陈，你拖何去？”二人互争不开，打入府堂上去。尤曰：“是我物，他强争。”丘亦曰：“是他争我物。”太爷曰：“你两人互争，各有甚记号？”丘曰：“我自买来的，未作记号。”尤曰：“我毡条内打有印记。”当堂开视，尤取衣带中木印对之，果相同。太府曰：“此是尤某之物，丘何得冒争！”将丘打十板，令尤领铺陈去，各赶出府外。丘骂曰：“你这贼是何人，敢如此骗我？后必报之！”尤五曰：“适船间你说尤刁民者，即是我。我与你何干，而终日道我刁？故教训你，刁人是这等做耳！”丘心中方悔：“是我妄称人恶，故致此失也。”
paragraphs.en: In the evening the boat reached shore; each man gathered his own luggage and left. You the Shyster tagged after Young Qiu. When they came before the prefectural offices, he snatched the bedding off the servant’s carrying pole and said: “Thanks for carrying it; I will drag it myself.” Young Qiu came to snatch it back and said: “This is my bedding—where are you dragging it?” The two fought without yielding, and the fight went up into the prefectural hall. You said: “It is my thing; he is forcing a claim.” Qiu also said: “He is seizing my thing.” His Honor said: “You two each claim it; what mark does each of you have?” Qiu said: “I bought it myself; I made no mark.” You said: “I stamped a seal inside the felt.” They opened it in court; You took the wood seal from his sash and matched it, and it was the same. The prefect said: “This is You’s thing. How can Qiu falsely claim it?” He had Qiu given ten strokes, ordered You to take the bedding, and drove them both out of the offices. Qiu cursed: “You thief, who are you, that you dare cheat me like this? I will pay you back later!” You Wu said: “On the boat just now you spoke of You the Shyster—that is me. What had I to do with you, that you spent the day calling me a shyster? So I taught you a lesson: this is how a shyster works!” Only then did Qiu regret in his heart: “I spoke of a man’s evil at random, and so brought this loss on myself.”

paragraphs.zh: 按：刁恶者，人谁不憎？但未识其人，勿轻扬其过。彼或从旁听之，必致恨于心。待你有失处，乘其隙而毒之，使人不自知矣。故古人三缄其口而慎其言。庞公遗安之计，但称曰好。彼尤五虽恶，何丘后生背地谈之，而自取尤五白占铺陈？与庞公遗安之计异矣。故孔子恶称人之恶，孟氏惕言人之不善者，皆圣贤教人远怨之道，言不可不慎也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Who does not hate a litigious villain? But if you do not know the man, do not lightly spread his faults. He may be listening from the side, and will surely store hatred in his heart. When you have a weak point, he will take the opening and poison you, and you will not even know it. That is why the ancients sealed their mouths three times and were careful of their words. Pangong’s plan for leaving peace to his descendants was simply to call everyone good. You Wu was evil, to be sure; but why did young Qiu talk of him behind his back, and bring on You Wu’s open seizure of the bedding? That is a far cry from Pangong’s plan for leaving peace. So Confucius disliked those who spoke of others’ faults, and Mencius was wary of talking of others’ lack of goodness: both are the way of sages and worthies teaching people to keep far from resentment. Words must not be used carelessly.

stories.title_en: He Slaps a Plaster over the Face and Snatches an Ingot

paragraphs.zh: 县城有一银匠，家颇殷实，解户领秋粮银，常托其倾煎。一日倾煎元宝，心内尚有系未透处，夜间又煮洗之。其铺门有一大缝，外可窥见其内。一棍买一大膏药，夜间潜往窥之。见其把两元宝洗讫，放于炉边，棍在外作叫痛声，呼曰：“开门！”银匠问曰：“是谁？”棍外答曰：“被赃坯打得重，求你炉边灼一膏药贴之。”银匠开门与入。棍作瘸行状，且手战呼痛，蓬头俯视，以一大膏药在炉边灼开，把两手望银匠当面一贴，即抢一元宝以逃。银匠不胜热痛，急扯下膏药，元宝已被其窃一去矣。急叫：“有贼！”且出门追赶，不知从哪路去。彷徨追过数十步，只得怅恨而归。
paragraphs.en: In the county town there was a silversmith, fairly well off. The tax-silver handlers who took in the autumn-grain silver often trusted him to melt and cast it. One day he was melting sycee ingots; some spots inside were still not fully worked through, so at night he boiled and washed them again. The shop door had a large crack; from outside one could see in. A crook bought a large plaster and at night crept up to peek. He saw the man finish washing two ingots and set them by the furnace. The crook outside made sounds of pain and called: “Open the door!” The silversmith asked: “Who is it?” The crook answered from outside: “I was beaten badly by a dirty brute. I beg you to let me heat a plaster by your furnace and stick it on.” The silversmith opened the door and let him in. The crook pretended to limp, and with shaking hands cried pain, hair in a mess, looking down. He heated a large plaster by the furnace until it opened, slapped it with both hands straight onto the silversmith’s face, then grabbed one ingot and fled. The silversmith could not bear the burning pain; he hurriedly tore the plaster off, but one ingot had already been stolen. He shouted, “Thief!” and went out to chase, but did not know which way the man had gone. He ran in confusion for several dozen steps, then could only go home sick with hate.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此棍装痛呼门及炉边灼膏药，情果难察。但元宝重物，须先收藏，然后开门则可无失矣。后人观此，凡有银在身者，皆不可轻容异色人得近旁也。
paragraphs.en: Note: This crook pretended to be in pain, called for the door, and heated a plaster by the furnace—the manner was indeed hard to see through. But an ingot is a heavy thing; he ought first to have put it away, and then opened the door, and there would have been no loss. Later readers, looking at this: anyone who has silver on him must not lightly let a strange-looking person come near.

stories.title_en: A Thief Blinds Them with Lime and Takes the Packets

paragraphs.zh: 孙滔，河南人也。常买绵布，在福建建宁府卖。一夜，在银匠王六店煎银，倾煎已讫，时对二包在桌。二人复在对银，有一盗径入其铺，将石灰撒其目。二人救目不暇，盗即将桌上所包之银拿走。滔拼命赶去，将及，盗乃丢一包于地。滔拾包归，到银铺开视之，则皆铁矣。后竟无迹可捕也。
paragraphs.en: Sun Tao was a man of Henan. He often bought cotton cloth and sold it in Jianning Prefecture in Fujian. One night he was at silversmith Wang Liu’s shop melting silver. The melting was done, and two packets sat facing each other on the table. The two men were still checking the silver when a thief walked straight into the shop and threw lime into their eyes. The two had no time but to save their eyes; the thief took the packaged silver off the table and left. Tao chased with all his life. He was about to catch him when the thief dropped one packet on the ground. Tao picked up the packet and went back; when he opened it at the silversmith’s, it was all iron. After that there was no trace by which to catch him.

paragraphs.zh: 按：语云：“贼是小人，智过君子。”诚哉是言也！其始入铺，撒灰腌人之目，致人无暇顾其财；追将近身、丢包于地，乃杜赶以脱其身也。此岂贼窥伺之机熟，而慢藏诲盗？然滔之不谨于其素，有以致之矣。鉴此惩噎，是为得之。
paragraphs.en: Note: The saying goes, “A thief is a small man, but his wit outruns a gentleman.” How true that is! When he first entered the shop, he threw lime to sting their eyes, so they had no time to look to their money; when the chase had nearly reached him, he dropped a packet on the ground, to stop the pursuit and slip away. Was this only because the thief’s watching and waiting were ripe, and careless storage invites thieves? Yet Tao’s usual want of care had brought it on. Take this as a warning from choking, and you will have it right.

stories.title_en: Crooks Strip Him at the Latrine in Open Day

paragraphs.zh: 王亨，南京扬州府人，是本府典吏。二考已满，该上京办事。家贫无措，措借亲朋银十馀两，独往北京，为办事使用。始到京中，在教军场边草坪中大解。方脱下裤，陡被二棍拿住，且骂且剥曰：“你这贼偷我衣物来。”即把其衣服并银一时抢去逃走。待他起来，缚裤赶之，二棍逃已远矣。亨行路日久，力已疲倦，拼死赶他不上，懊恨冲天，只得在会同馆乞借盘缠回家，另作区处。
paragraphs.en: Wang Heng was a man of Yangzhou Prefecture under Nanjing, a clerk in that prefecture. His two terms of clerical service were up, and he was due to go to the capital for assignment. The family was poor and had no means; he borrowed a little more than ten taels from kin and friends and went alone to Beijing, for use in the assignment. Just after he reached the capital, he was relieving himself on the grass by the drill ground. He had just dropped his trousers when two crooks seized him, cursing and stripping him: “You thief, you stole our clothes.” They snatched his clothes and silver at once and ran. By the time he got up, tied his trousers, and chased them, the two crooks were already far off. Heng had been on the road many days and was worn out; he chased with all his life and could not catch them. Sick with hate that filled the sky, he could only go to the Huitongguan guesthouse and beg travel money to go home, and make other plans later.

paragraphs.zh: 按：孤客出外，非唯僻处可防劫夺，即大路解手之际，必当以裤脱之，挟在腋下。倘遇光棍若行歹意，则起而逃之亦可，或与之交战亦可。若王亨者，不知提防，而被棍将衣银尽剥一空。斯时也，盘缠无觅，顾何前程？苟非会同馆中同道辈乞借盘缠而归，几为乞丐矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: A lone traveler abroad should guard against robbery not only in lonely places. Even on a main road, when relieving himself, he must take the trousers off and hold them under his arm. If crooks then mean harm, he can get up and run, or he can fight them. As for Wang Heng, he did not know to guard, and the crooks stripped him of clothes and silver down to nothing. At that moment he had no travel money to find—what of his future post? If fellow clerks at the Huitongguan had not lent him travel money to go home, he would nearly have become a beggar.

stories.title_en: Boatmen Abscond with a Servant and the Baggage

paragraphs.zh: 倪典史以吏员出身，家实巨富。初受官，将赴新任，在京置买器用什物、珍玩缎匹，色色美丽，装作行李六担。打点俱备，先遣三个家人押往江边搭船，以一家人在船中守护，其二人复归。次日，同倪典史大伙人俱到江边寻船，并不见前船；其守船家人不知载在何去，知被贼艄所拐矣。
paragraphs.en: Assistant Magistrate Ni had risen from the clerical ranks; the family was in fact hugely rich. On first receiving office, about to go to his new post, he bought in the capital utensils and household goods, curios, and bolts of silk, every kind fine and beautiful, packed as six loads of luggage. When everything was ready, he first sent three servants to the river to hire a boat; one servant stayed on the boat to watch, and the other two came back. The next day Assistant Magistrate Ni and the rest of the party all went to the river to look for the boat, and the earlier boat was nowhere to be seen. The servant who had been watching the boat had been carried off no one knew where; they knew a thief of a boatman had abducted them.

paragraphs.zh: 倪典史不得已，复入京城，向乡知借觅盘缠，欲往在京衙门告捕船贼。同选乡友阻之曰：“凡讨船须在捕头写定，其舵公有姓名可查，方保稳当。若自向江头讨船，彼此不相识，来历无可查，安得不致失误？且江边常有贼船，舵公伪装商贾，打听某船有好货，多致江中劫掠者，皆是在头查访去。若不识者，误上他船，虽主人亦同被害，何况载走一仆乎！今你赴任有限期，岂能在此久待？船贼又无名姓踪影，虽告何从追捕？不如罢休。”倪典史依劝，复在京中再置切要之物，急往赴任也。此不识写船而致误者，故述为舟行之戒。
paragraphs.en: Assistant Magistrate Ni had no choice but to go back into the capital and borrow travel money from fellow provincials, intending to file a charge at a capital yamen and have the boat thieves caught. Fellow new appointees stopped him, saying: “Whenever you hire a boat you should register it at the licensed wharf office, so the helmsman has a name that can be looked up; only then is it safe. If you hire a boat yourself at the river’s edge, neither side knows the other, and there is no origin to check—how can you not come to grief? Besides, there are often thief-boats along the river. Helmsmen disguise themselves as merchants, find out which boat has good cargo, and many then rob it mid-river—those are all cases of failing to check at the office first. If you do not know this and board their boat by mistake, even the master himself may be harmed with them—how much more when they carry off one servant! You have a deadline to take up your post; how can you wait here long? The boat thieves have no names or traces; even if you file a charge, from where would you hunt them? Better drop it.” Assistant Magistrate Ni followed the advice, bought the most needful things again in the capital, and hurried off to his post. This is a case of not knowing how to book a boat, and so coming to grief; I record it as a warning for those who travel by water.

stories.title_en: The Bride Escapes the Boat by Night

paragraphs.zh: 扬州有一危棍，以骗局为生。生一女危氏，美貌聪明，年方二八，尚未字人。同帮计棍，青年伶俐，家无父母，危棍因以女招赘为婿。夫妻欢爱，岳婿同心。
paragraphs.en: In Yangzhou there was a crook named Wei, who lived by swindles. He had a daughter, Miss Wei, pretty and clever, just sixteen, not yet betrothed. A partner in the same trade, Crook Ji, was a young man of ready wits, with no parents at home; Crook Wei therefore took him as a live-in son-in-law. Husband and wife loved each other, and father-in-law and son-in-law were of one mind.

paragraphs.zh: 后半年内，无甚生意。适有贾知县新受官赴任，经过扬州，欲娶一妾。危与计私议，欲以女脱嫁之。计许诺，自为媒，往与贾爷议。来看称意，即行聘礼，受银八十两，择日成婚。危与计同对女曰：“今半年无生意，家用穷迫，故以你假嫁与贾知县。其实你夫少年人，何忍舍你？我为父母，止生你一人，何忍舍你去？只不得已，把你为货也。况贾爷年老，他眼下未带长妻来，自然爱惜你。但恐到任后，接长妻到，必然酷虐你，骂詈鞭挞，自是不免。自古道：‘宁作贫人妻，莫作贵人妾’。今暂送你去，不日即登船矣。你夫暗以船随行，其船夜挂一白裤为号。你夜间若可逃，即逃过白裤船来，夫即在接你矣。切莫贪睡，误你夫终身；且你自受苦楚。”计故挽妻衣，涕泣面恳曰：“你肯许归，任你去；若不能逃，吾宁与你同死，决不忍相舍。”危氏亦泣曰：“父母有命，怎的不归？只你要随船候接，不可耽误。”三人商议已定。
paragraphs.en: For half a year after that there was little business. It happened that Magistrate Jia, newly appointed and on his way to his post, passed through Yangzhou and wanted to take a concubine. Wei and Ji talked it over in private, and wanted to fake-marry the daughter to him. Ji agreed, acted as matchmaker himself, and went to discuss it with His Honor Jia. Jia came to look, was pleased, sent betrothal gifts at once, paid eighty taels, and chose a day for the wedding. Wei and Ji together said to the daughter: “We have had no business for half a year; the household is hard pressed, so we are fake-marrying you to Magistrate Jia. In truth your husband is a young man—how could he bear to give you up? We are your parents, and we have only you—how could we bear to let you go? We simply have no choice; we are using you as goods. Besides, His Honor Jia is old; he has not brought his principal wife with him for now, so of course he will cherish you. But I fear that after he takes up his post and sends for the principal wife, she will surely treat you cruelly; cursing and whipping will be hard to avoid. The old saying goes: ‘Better a poor man’s wife than a rich man’s concubine.’ For now we will send you; in a few days he will board a boat. Your husband will secretly follow in a boat, with a white pair of trousers hung up as a signal. If you can flee at night, flee across to the white-trousers boat; your husband will be there to take you. Do not sleep greedily and ruin your husband’s whole life; you yourself would also suffer.” Ji deliberately clutched his wife’s clothes, weeping, and pleaded to her face: “If you will promise to come back, I will let you go; if you cannot flee, I would rather die with you—I cannot bear to part.” Miss Wei also wept and said: “When father and mother have given the order, how would I not come back? Only you must follow in a boat and wait to take me; do not miss the time.” The three of them had the plan set.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，贾知县遣人迎婚，计为媒送去，贾与危氏在店成亲。又次日，危亦备席待婿，兼为起程。第四日，贾同妻收拾上船，危、计二人送别殷勤。船行一日无恙，次日泊于洲渚。计暗以船随，挨附其旁，挂一白裤于上。危氏同贾夫出船头观玩，见白裤船在旁，知计夫在候矣。夜与贾宿，着意绸缪，尽云雨之欢。贾以暮年新娶，夜夜不虚；况此夜船中又尽兴一次，帖然鼾睡矣。危氏遂密起，爬过有白裤船。计夫早已在候，相见欢甚，正似花再重开月再圆也。夤夜撑船逃回。
paragraphs.en: The next day Magistrate Jia sent men to receive the bride. Ji as matchmaker saw her off; Jia and Miss Wei consummated the marriage at an inn. The day after that, Wei also laid a feast for his son-in-law, and for the start of the journey as well. On the fourth day Jia and his wife packed and boarded; Wei and Ji saw them off with great care. The boat went one day without incident. The next day it moored at a sandbar. Ji secretly followed in a boat, drew up alongside, and hung a white pair of trousers on it. Miss Wei went out to the bow with husband Jia to look about, saw the white-trousers boat beside them, and knew husband Ji was waiting. That night she slept with Jia, put her whole mind to tenderness, and they made love to the full. Jia was old and newly married, and had not missed a night; besides, this night on the boat he spent himself once more, and then slept snoring soundly. Miss Wei then rose in secret, crawled across to the boat with the white trousers. Husband Ji had long been waiting; they were overjoyed to see each other, just as if the flower had opened again and the moon were round once more. In the night they poled away and fled home.

paragraphs.zh: 次早，贾知县醒来，不见危氏，心甚疑怪。再差一家人，往危老家报。危家惊异，疑是船中乖争，致逼投水，即赴府具状，告苛逼溺命事。家人数日回报，贾知县欲赴任期，不能久待，亦不往诉辨，自径投任去。三年后，入京朝觐，差家人送些少仪物与危老，见其家有一少妇，抱一幼子，宛似危氏，驰归报主。及贾知县打轿往，并不见踪。问昨妇何人，危云：“妻姨之女。”其妻反出来涕泣诘骂，扭问取人，又被骗银十两，方得脱身。此误娶棍女而人财两空，又受尽多少闲气也。
paragraphs.en: The next morning Magistrate Jia woke and did not see Miss Wei; he was much puzzled and suspicious. He then sent a servant to report it at Old Wei’s house. The Wei family acted startled, and suspected a quarrel on the boat had driven her to throw herself in the water. They went at once to the prefecture and filed a charge of cruelty driving a person to drown. After several days the servant came back to report. Magistrate Jia had a deadline to take up his post and could not wait long; he did not go to plead his side, but went straight to his post. Three years later he went to the capital for the imperial audience, and sent a servant with a few ceremonial gifts to Old Wei. The servant saw that the house had a young woman holding a small child, the very image of Miss Wei, and galloped back to tell his master. When Magistrate Jia went in a sedan, there was no trace of her. He asked who yesterday’s woman was; Wei said: “My wife’s sister’s daughter.” Wei’s wife then came out weeping, questioning and cursing, twisting him to produce the person; he was cheated of another ten taels before he could get away. This is a case of wrongly taking a crook’s daughter: he lost both the person and the money, and swallowed no small amount of idle abuse besides.

paragraphs.zh: 按：娶妾于妻岳之家，既在店成亲，又送别登舟，可谓极稳矣。谁知在船后，夜复能逃？故在外娶妾，不唯审择外家，兼亦宜审媒人居止，及靠店家一同核实，方可无失。然大抵不及娶本地人女，为更稳也。
paragraphs.en: Note: He took a concubine from the girl’s father’s house; they consummated the marriage at an inn, and were even seen off onto the boat—one would call it extremely safe. Who knew that later, on the boat, she could still flee at night? So when you take a concubine away from home, you should not only look into the girl’s family; you should also look into where the matchmaker lives, and have the innkeeper join in checking the facts, and only then will there be no loss. But in the main it is still safer to take a local girl.

stories.title_en: Boatmen Kill a Merchant Whose Copper Looked Like Treasure

paragraphs.zh: 罗四维，南京凤阳府临淮县人。同仆程三郎，带银一百餘两往松江买梭布，往福建建宁府卖，复往崇安买笋。其年笋少价贵，即将银在此处买走乌铜物，并三夹杯盘诸项铜器，用竹箱盛贮，并行李装作三担。崇安发夫，直到水口陈四店写船。陡遇表亲林子达，亦在此店中。达问：“买甚货物？”维曰：“只买些铜器去，更带杯盘等，欲留家用。”达同牙人陈四，代讨一箭船。舵公赖富二、水手李彩、翁暨得搬其行李上船，甚重，舵公疑是金银，乃起不良心，一上船后，再不搭人。维曰：“我要速去，何如不搭人？”舵公曰：“今将晚矣。明日随搭数人，便开船。”维叫三郎买些酒菜，今晚饮用。舵工与水手三人商议：“今晚错过机会，明日不好动手。”维与仆饮醉熟睡。半夜后，舵公将船移于闲处，三人将他主仆以刀砍死，丢尸于江。打开打看，乃是铜物，止现银壹十五两。富二曰：“我说都是银子，三人一场富贵。原来是这东西！”彩曰：“有这等好货物，也多值银。”富二曰：“发在何处去卖？”彩曰：“何愁无卖处？可安船在一处，沿途发卖，岂无人买？”
paragraphs.en: Luo Siwei was a man of Linhuai County in Fengyang Prefecture, under Nanjing. With his servant Cheng Sanlang he took a little more than a hundred taels, went to Songjiang to buy cotton cloth, sold it in Jianning Prefecture in Fujian, then went on to Chong’an to buy bamboo shoots. That year shoots were scarce and dear, so he used the silver there to buy blackened copperware, and also laminated cups and plates and other copper pieces. He packed them in bamboo chests, and with the luggage made three loads. From Chong’an he sent porters all the way to Chen Si’s shop at Shuikou to book a boat. There he suddenly met a cousin, Lin Zida, also in this shop. Zida asked: “What goods did you buy?” Siwei said: “Only some copperware to take, and also cups and plates I want to keep for the house.” Zida and the broker Chen Si hired an arrow-boat for him. The helmsman Lai Fuer and the sailors Li Cai and Weng Jide moved his luggage on board; it was very heavy. The helmsman suspected it was gold and silver, and a bad thought rose in him. Once they were on board he would take no more passengers. Siwei said: “I want to leave quickly—why take no one else?” The helmsman said: “It is almost evening now. Tomorrow we will take a few more and then cast off.” Siwei told Sanlang to buy some wine and food for tonight. The helmsman and the two sailors talked it over: “If we miss the chance tonight, tomorrow we cannot act.” Siwei and his servant drank themselves drunk and slept soundly. After midnight the helmsman moved the boat to a quiet spot; the three men cut master and servant to death with knives and threw the bodies in the river. They broke open the loads and looked: it was copperware, and only fifteen taels of ready silver. Fuer said: “I said it was all silver—a fortune for the three of us. And it turns out to be this stuff!” Cai said: “Goods this fine are still worth a good deal of silver.” Fuer said: “Where can we send them to sell?” Cai said: “Why worry about a place to sell? Moor the boat somewhere and sell along the way—will no one buy?”

paragraphs.zh: 林子达与四维分袂之后，已三个月矣，始到家中往拜四维。维父曰：“小儿出门，尚未归。”达曰：“差矣！”三月前，我在江西水口，同他在牙人陈四店相会。我与牙人同他去讨船，说他在福建买铜货，以竹箱装作三担，竟归来本处发脱。莫非舵公行歹意乎？”言未毕，父母妻子举家大哭。达曰：“且勿哭，倘在途中发卖也未可知。或舵公行歹意，必以铜物卖各处。试往各店踪迹铜物，问其来历，便见明白。纵铜物无踪，再到水口牙人陈四家，寻舵公问之，必得下落。”维父然之，叫次子罗逵随达去访。
paragraphs.en: It was already three months after Lin Zida had parted from Siwei when Zida reached home and went to call on Siwei. Siwei’s father said: “My son went out and has not yet come back.” Zida said: “That is wrong! Three months ago I met him at broker Chen Si’s shop at Shuikou in Jiangxi. I went with the broker to hire a boat for him. He said he had bought copper goods in Fujian, packed in bamboo chests as three loads, and was coming straight home to this place to sell them. Can it be the helmsman meant harm?” Before he had finished, father, mother, wife, and the whole house burst into tears. Zida said: “Do not cry yet. He may still be selling along the way, for all we know. Or if the helmsman meant harm, he would have to sell the copper in various places. Try tracing the copper in the shops, ask where it came from, and the matter will be clear. Even if the copper leaves no trace, go on to broker Chen Si’s at Shuikou, find the helmsman and question him, and you will surely get the bottom of it.” Siwei’s father agreed, and told his second son Luo Kui to go with Zida to inquire.

paragraphs.zh: 访至芜湖县，铺中见其铜物，即问：“此铜物是公自买的，抑或他客贩来发行的？”铺主曰：“三月前，有三个客人来卖者。”达曰：“何处人？”曰：“江西人。”达惊惶曰：“差矣，失手是实。”即同逵径至水口，问陈四曰：“前装表亲货物的舵公，是何处人？”陈四曰：“沿山县人。”达道其故，即同陈四到沿山捕捉。
paragraphs.en: They inquired as far as Wuhu County. In a shop they saw the copperware, and asked: “Did you buy this copper yourself, or did some other merchant bring it to sell?” The shopkeeper said: “Three months ago three guests came and sold it.” Zida said: “Men of what place?” He said: “Jiangxi men.” Zida was alarmed: “This is wrong—we have truly lost him.” He went with Kui straight to Shuikou and asked Chen Si: “The helmsman who loaded my cousin’s goods—what place was he from?” Chen Si said: “A man of Yanshan County.” Zida told him why, and went with Chen Si to Yanshan to seize them.

paragraphs.zh: 斯时，李彩、翁暨得卖得铜器，银入手，各在妓家去嫖。林、陈窥见彩，即躲之。林子达曰：“他在院中取乐，必不便动。我与你往县去告，差捕兵缉拿，恕不漏网。”二人入县告准，陈爷差捕兵六名，同林、陈往院中去捕缉。彩与得二人正与妓笑饮，陈四指与捕兵，俱擒锁之。再到赖富家来，富方出门他适，遇见亦被捉获。三人同拿到官，陈爷审问，将三人夹敲，受苦不过，只得招认。彩曰：“彼时搬箱上船，其重非常。疑是金银，三人方起意谋之，将尸丢落于江。开其箱看，尽是铜物，只得现银一拾五两，悔之无及。铜物沿途卖讫，银已分散。今其事败，是我等自作自受，甘认死罪。”陈爷将三人各打五十板，即拟典刑，赃追与罗逵、林子达领归。二人叩首而去。
paragraphs.en: At that time Li Cai and Weng Jide had sold the copperware, had the silver in hand, and had each gone to a brothel to wench. Lin and Chen caught sight of Cai and hid. Lin Zida said: “He is taking his pleasure in the house; he will not be in a hurry to move. You and I will go to the county to file a charge, and have constables sent to seize them, so they cannot slip the net.” The two went into the county; the charge was accepted. His Honor Chen sent six constables, who went with Lin and Chen to the brothel to arrest them. Cai and Jide were just laughing and drinking with the prostitutes; Chen Si pointed them out to the constables, and both were seized and locked. They then went to Lai Fu’s house; Fu was just going out elsewhere, met them, and was also caught. The three were taken together before the official. His Honor Chen examined them, put them in the ankle-press and beat them; they could not bear the pain and had to confess. Cai said: “At the time we moved the chests on board they were extraordinarily heavy. We thought it was gold and silver, so the three of us formed the intent to kill them, and threw the bodies in the river. We opened the chests and looked: all copperware, only fifteen taels of ready silver. Regret came too late. The copper was sold along the way; the silver has already been split. Now the affair is out; we brought it on ourselves, and willingly admit a capital crime.” His Honor Chen had each of the three given fifty strokes, then sentenced them to death; the stolen goods were recovered and given to Luo Kui and Lin Zida to take home. The two kowtowed and left.

paragraphs.zh: 按：溪河本险危之地，舵公多蠢暴之徒。若带实银在身，须深藏严防。或带铜器铅锡等物，镇重类银，须明与说之，开与见之，以免其垂涎，方保安全。不然，逐金丸以弹雀，指薏苡为明珠，其不来奸人之睥睨者几希。若维仇之能报，犹幸子达之得其根脚也。使非因写船者以穷其舵公，何以歼罪人而殄厥慝乎？然诛逆何如保躬？死偿何如生还？故出行而带重物者，宜借鉴于斯而慎之密之，其永无失矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Streams and rivers are dangerous places by nature, and helmsmen are often coarse, violent men. If you carry ready silver on you, you must hide it deep and watch it strictly. If you carry copper, lead, tin, and the like—heavy things that resemble silver—you must tell them plainly, open the loads and show them, so they will not drool, and only then will you be safe. Otherwise it is like shooting sparrows with gold pellets, or pointing at coix seeds and calling them pearls: few will escape the greedy stares of villains. As for Siwei’s feud being avenged, it was still luck that Zida got the man’s origin. If they had not used the man who booked the boat to track down the helmsman, how could they have wiped out the guilty and cut off the evil? But punishing rebels is not as good as keeping your own person; death repaid is not as good as coming home alive. So those who travel and carry heavy goods should take a lesson from this, be careful and close, and they will never come to grief.

stories.title_en: Heavy Mirrors on Board Draw a Murder Plot

paragraphs.zh: 熊镐，章富人，乃世家子也。力足扼虎，兼习棍棒。尝月夜挟二婢往后园，遇一虎跳墙入，即退入家，各持钢叉、大杖出。虎对面扑来，镐以叉抵，顺放于地，急打一下。虎复再扑，镐又叉放之，再打一下，虎遂回身而去。镐从后赶打，虎为之倒。疾呼二婢曰：“速来助。”二婢各以大杖以鏖之，虎立死杖下。时称之曰“打虎镐四官”。
paragraphs.en: Xiong Hao of Zhangfu was a son of a hereditary official house. He was strong enough to hold a tiger, and had also practiced staff and club. Once on a moonlit night he took two maids to the back garden and met a tiger that had jumped over the wall. He went back into the house at once; each took a steel fork or a heavy staff and came out. The tiger sprang at them face to face; Hao blocked it with the fork, laid the fork down, and struck once. The tiger sprang again; Hao again used the fork and then struck once more; the tiger turned and left. Hao chased it from behind and beat it; the tiger fell. He quickly called the two maids: “Come help at once.” Each maid used a heavy staff and they laid on together; the tiger died under the staves. People at the time called him “Fourth Master Hao the Tiger-Beater.”

paragraphs.zh: 后思遍游各胜处，故脱兄云：“将出外买卖。”兄阻之曰：“汝刚而无谋，莫思赚钱，还恐生祸。”镐曰：“老仆满起有力多智，与我同去，何妨？”兄不能阻。镐带百餘金行，曰：“吾出外相机置货，虽不得利，岂折本乎？有谁人欺得我者！”及游浙粤，有货可买者，仆满起曰：“此价甚廉，买归必得利。”镐曰：“吾远到此，未遍览此中景致，若遂置货，安能轻身自由？”仆累禀几次，皆不见听，知其志在浪游，不思利也，后只任之，主饮亦饮，主行亦随。不半年，本去三分之二矣。起复曰：“不归将无盘缠。”镐曰：“本虽少，亦要置些货归，可当远回人事相送者。”又挨两月，到湖州，起又催归。镐曰：“买何物好？”起曰：“笔墨上好。”镐曰：“不在行不会拣择，恐受人亏。亦须更买甚物，与母嫂及我妻者？银本已折，省他辈多口。”起曰：“细缎、镜好。”镐曰：“细缎无多本，不是这般客。不如买十两笔墨，十两镜罢。”起曰：“亦好。”催趱买归，只两小箱。镐曰：“此货甚妙，又简便易带。”
paragraphs.en: Later he wanted to tour all the famous places, so he told his elder brother: “I am going out to trade.” His brother stopped him: “You are hard and have no cunning. Do not think of making money; I fear you will only make trouble.” Hao said: “The old servant Man Qi has strength and much wit; if he goes with me, what harm?” His brother could not stop him. Hao took a little more than a hundred taels and set out, saying: “I will go out and buy goods as the chance comes. Even if I make no profit, how should I lose the capital? Who can take advantage of me?” When they toured Zhejiang and Guangdong, and there were goods worth buying, the servant Man Qi said: “This price is very cheap; if we buy and take it home we will surely profit.” Hao said: “I have come a long way and have not yet seen all the sights here. If I buy goods at once, how can I travel light and free?” The servant reported it several times and was never heard; he knew his master’s mind was on idle touring, not on profit, and afterward only let him be: when the master drank, he drank; when the master went, he followed. In less than half a year two thirds of the capital was gone. Qi said again: “If we do not go home we will have no travel money.” Hao said: “Though the capital is small, we still must buy some goods to take back, to serve as gifts after a long journey.” They delayed another two months and reached Huzhou; Qi again urged him home. Hao said: “What should we buy?” Qi said: “Brushes and ink are best.” Hao said: “I am not in that trade and cannot choose; I fear I will be taken advantage of. We also need to buy something for Mother, my sister-in-law, and my wife. The capital is already lost; let us spare them extra talk.” Qi said: “Fine silks and mirrors would be good.” Hao said: “We have not much capital for silks; we are not that kind of merchant. Better buy ten taels of brushes and ink and ten taels of mirrors.” Qi said: “That will do too.” They hurried the purchase for the return; there were only two small chests. Hao said: “These goods are excellent, and also light and easy to carry.”

paragraphs.zh: 及到江边搭船，舵公见财主威仪，家人齐整，奈何行李只两小箱。及抬入船中，觉箱中镇重，想必尽是银也。故以言动问曰：“客官从何来，亦不多买些货物？”镐以本少，恐客商见轻，故谎言：“吾家兄敝任在湖广，吾从任中归，未买得甚货。”舵公曰：“原来是大舍。”又见家人伏侍恭敬，每呼主为相公，使用皆大手面，不与诸商一类，以此益信为真官舍，船中人皆敬让之。及到岸，诸商都搬起船。舵公独留熊大舍曰：“船中客官多，未能伸敬。念备一杯酒，敬请大舍。”即上岸，多买佳肴美酒，夜间劝饮，甚是殷勤，熊镐宽心放饮。舵公又苦劝家人酒。满起心知其非好意，初诈推不饮，后难禁其劝，亦饮数杯，推醉去睡。熊舍凭舵公劝饮，真醉不醒事。起俟其睡熟，即起对舵公曰：“吾非真醉。今将近家，心中忧闷，吃酒不下耳。此相公酒色之徒。大相公在任中，将几百两银打发他归。在路上嫖用都尽，只带得几把笔，几面镜归，与侄子辈作人事耳。明日大老爷归，必责我不能谏阻。世有此人，见酒如糖，又好夸口，怎么谏他？我试开两箱与你看，其中哪有厘银？”即取锁匙开两箱，惟笔与镜，并无银两。起取两面镜送舵公，曰：“一路来多蒙照顾，各送一镜与你用。”舵公曰：“主物不可擅送人。”起曰：“拿一半去，他也理不得，到家后那晓得数。”复锁住箱，与舵公去睡，起一夜提防。次日上岸，熊曰：“难得舵公如此好意，再偿他银一钱。”
paragraphs.en: When they hired a boat at the river, the helmsman saw a rich man’s bearing and servants in good order, yet the luggage was only two small chests. When they were lifted into the boat he felt how heavy the chests were, and thought they must be all silver. So he probed with words: “Where have you come from, sir? And you did not buy more goods?” Hao, because his capital was small, feared other merchants would look down on him, so he lied: “My elder brother holds a humble post in Huguang. I am returning from his post and did not buy much.” The helmsman said: “So you are a young gentleman.” He also saw the servants wait on him with respect, always calling their master “young sir,” and that he spent in a large style, not of a kind with ordinary merchants; for this he believed still more that he was truly a young gentleman of an official house, and everyone on the boat deferred to him. When they reached shore, the other merchants all moved off the boat. The helmsman alone kept Young Gentleman Xiong, saying: “There were many guests on the boat; I could not show respect. I have prepared a cup of wine; please let me invite you.” He went ashore, bought many fine dishes and good wine, pressed them to drink at night, most attentive; Xiong Hao drank with an easy heart. The helmsman also hard-pressed the servant to drink. Man Qi knew in his heart it was not kindly meant. At first he pretended to refuse; later he could not stop the urging, drank several cups, then pleaded drunkenness and went to sleep. Young Xiong let the helmsman press him, and was truly drunk and knew nothing. When Qi saw he was sound asleep, he got up and said to the helmsman: “I am not truly drunk. We are near home now; my heart is heavy, and I cannot get the wine down. This young master is a man of wine and women. The elder master, in his post, sent him home with several hundred taels. On the road he spent it all on whoring; he is only taking a few brushes and a few mirrors home as gifts for the nephews. Tomorrow the old master will come home and will surely blame me for not stopping him. There are men like this in the world: they see wine as sugar, and love to boast—how can I check him? Let me open the two chests and show you: is there a speck of silver in them?” He took the key and opened both chests: only brushes and mirrors, no silver at all. Qi took two mirrors and gave them to the helmsman, saying: “All along the way you have looked after us; I give each of you a mirror to use.” The helmsman said: “A master’s things must not be given away.” Qi said: “Take half; he will not be able to make it out, and once we are home he will not know the count.” He locked the chests again, went with the helmsman to sleep, and kept watch all night. The next day they went ashore. Hao said: “It is rare for a helmsman to be so kind; give him another qian of silver.”

paragraphs.zh: 及归家，起曰：“可数过镜，勿令有失。”镐检过曰：“更失两面。”起曰：“吾将这两面镜，换你我两颗头归。主人尚未知乎？”镐曰：“你何狂言？”起将船中劝饮事，一一叙之，曰：“彼非欲谋害，将别之人，何如此更费酒馔，若殷勤乎？”镐惊曰：“是也！非尔知事，险丧二命耳！”一家人闻之皆喜，赏满起。
paragraphs.en: When they reached home, Qi said: “Count the mirrors, so none are missing.” Hao checked and said: “Two more are gone.” Qi said: “I traded those two mirrors for your head and mine to come home. Does the master still not know?” Hao said: “Why this wild talk?” Qi told the affair of the drinking on the boat, item by item, and said: “If he did not mean to murder us, why would he spend extra on wine and food for other people, and be so attentive?” Hao was startled: “So it was! If you had not known how to act, we would nearly have lost two lives!” The whole household heard and was glad, and rewarded Man Qi.

paragraphs.zh: 按：镐本膏粱之子，以纵性为快，以夸口为高，哪知世路之险？若非满起心明，轻以二命付鱼腹耳。凡远行者，主若疏满，得一谨密家人，亦大有益。故旅以丧童仆为厉，以得童仆为吉。圣人系旅之义大矣哉。
paragraphs.en: Note: Hao was a son of rich food and fine clothes; he took following his nature as pleasure and boasting as high style, and did not know how dangerous the world’s roads are. If Man Qi had not had a clear mind, two lives would have been lightly given to the fishes’ bellies. Whenever you travel far, if the master is careless and slack, getting one close, careful servant is also a great benefit. So in the Travel hexagram, losing a servant is ominous, and gaining a servant is auspicious. How great is the Sage’s attached meaning for Travel!

stories.title_en: A Servant Puts the Bags on Another Boat by Mistake

paragraphs.zh: 陆梦麟，江西进贤人。往福建海澄县买胡椒十餘担，复往芜湖发卖。有一客伙，将硼砂一担对换，餘者以银伐之。次日，叫店家写舵公陈涯四船，直到建宁。诸货都搬入船，只一仆詹兴，挑实落行李一担，跟梦麟同行。途中陡遇一乡亲，动问家中事务，语喇喇不能休。乃命仆先担行李上船，再来此听使用。仆挑往别船去，收在船舱已讫，再来寻主，尚与乡亲谈叙未决。见仆来，即差之别干，始辞乡亲到船。查行李未见，即将家人打骂；又坐舵公偷去，状告本县胡爷，言舵公盗他卖胡椒银一百餘两，以店家祝念九作证。舵公诉：“船中有客商十数伙，哪见他仆挑行李上船？”胡爷拘来审问，同船众商都谈，未曾见挑甚行李。胡爷曰：“船不漏针。别货物都在，独行李有银便会失落？”将舵公敲夹，不认，曰：“是他仆詹兴见囊中有银，自盗去以陷我；或错担别船去，以致有失。小人虽夹死难招！”胡爷又审詹兴曰：“想是你错认别人船为己船，忙中有失，非你背主，好好招来免夹。”詹兴不认，乃夹敲一百。受苦不过，只得招认：“是主人路遇乡亲谈话，我自担上船去，藏入船舱讫，再回听主差唤。及到船，并未见行李。是我一时错认，以致有失。恐主人加罪于我，我故不敢承。望老爷救小人一命。”胡爷将詹兴责三十板，劝梦麟曰：“是你自错。凡出外为商，银物不可离身。当担行李时，须叫詹兴看守，待你到船，然后差别干；纵错上别船，亦不会失。今若此，是你命该失财，岂可以怨仆乎？”各发出免供。
paragraphs.en: Lu Menglin was a man of Jinxian in Jiangxi. He went to Haicheng County in Fujian, bought more than ten piculs of pepper, then went to Wuhu to sell it. A fellow merchant swapped a picul of borax; the rest was paid in silver. The next day he had the innkeeper book Helmsman Chen Yasi’s boat, going all the way to Jianning. All the goods were moved onto the boat; only one servant, Zhan Xing, carried a load of the real luggage and followed Menglin. On the way they suddenly met a fellow townsman; they asked about family affairs, and the talk rattled on and would not stop. So he ordered the servant to carry the luggage onto the boat first, then come back here and wait for orders. The servant carried it onto another boat, stowed it in the cabin, then came back to find his master, who was still talking with the townsman and had not finished. When he saw the servant come, he sent him on another errand, then took leave of the townsman and went to the boat. He checked and did not see the luggage, so he beat and cursed the servant; he also sat the theft on the helmsman, and filed a charge with His Honor Hu of the county, saying the helmsman had stolen more than a hundred taels of silver from the pepper sales, with innkeeper Zhu Nianjiu as witness. The helmsman stated: “There are a dozen-odd merchants on the boat; who saw his servant carry luggage on board?” His Honor Hu summoned them to hear the case; all the fellow merchants on the boat said they had not seen any luggage carried on. His Honor Hu said: “A boat does not leak a needle. The other goods are all here; only the luggage, which had silver, happens to be missing?” He put the helmsman in the press and beat him. The man would not confess, and said: “It was his servant Zhan Xing who saw there was silver in the bundle, stole it himself to trap me; or he carried it onto the wrong boat, and so it was lost. Even if you press this little man to death I will not confess!” His Honor Hu then examined Zhan Xing: “I think you mistook another man’s boat for your own, and in the hurry something was lost; it was not that you turned on your master. Confess properly and you will be spared the press.” Zhan Xing would not confess, so he was pressed and beaten a hundred blows. He could not bear the pain and had to confess: “My master met a fellow townsman on the road and was talking. I carried it onto a boat myself, hid it in the cabin, then went back to wait for my master’s orders. When we reached the boat, the luggage was not to be seen. I mistook it for a moment, and so it was lost. I feared my master would add to my punishment, so I dared not admit it. I beg Your Honor to spare this little man’s life.” His Honor Hu had Zhan Xing given thirty strokes, and advised Menglin: “This was your own mistake. Whenever you go out to trade, silver and goods must not leave your person. When the luggage was to be carried, you should have told Zhan Xing to watch it, and only sent him on other errands after you reached the boat; even if it went onto the wrong boat, it would not have been lost. Now that it has come to this, your fate was to lose the money—how can you resent the servant?” They were each sent out and spared further depositions.

paragraphs.zh: 按：货物上船，须不离人看守。要防舵公侵盗，又要得智仆为吉也。故雏仆之挑行节，银物所系，须跟在身边，托在实落，方无所失。若先令挑去，错寄别船，安能无失哉？然麟徒知叙旧之谈，致仆误丧其财而干讼者，何其愚也！诸商鉴此，可为后戒。
paragraphs.en: Note: When goods go onto a boat, you must not leave them unwatched. You have to guard against the helmsman stealing, and you also need a smart servant to be lucky. So when a greenhorn servant carries the travel bundle—the thing silver and goods hang on—he must follow at your side, and you must leave it only where it is secure, and then nothing will be lost. If you first tell him to carry it ahead, and it is wrongly left on another boat, how can there be no loss? Yet Menglin only knew how to talk over old times, and caused the servant to lose the money by mistake and drag them into a lawsuit—how foolish! Merchants should look at this and take it as a later warning.

stories.title_en: A Porter Dashes Off with Unloaded Cargo

paragraphs.zh: 建城溪边，凡客船到岸，众脚夫丛集，求雇担代挑入城。有老成客，必喝退众夫，待船货齐收上岸，都数纪定，然后分作几担，叫几名脚夫，自相识认，乃发入城，急令人跟行其后，方保无失。若雏家到，众脚夫不管物件检齐否，即为收拾上担，及急跟夫去，多致遗物在船中未尽收。
paragraphs.en: By the creek at Jianning city, whenever a guest boat reaches shore, porters swarm and beg to be hired to carry loads into the city.
